steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a graph learning paper that makes Subgraph GNNs more efficient by learning which subgraphs to select instead of using the full bag or sampling at random. Motivate the problem, introduce our Policy-learn architecture and its theory, and close with the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Subgraph GNNs and why they are popular
- Their computational cost and random sampling as a workaround
- Do we need all subgraphs? Figure 1 example
- Why random selection is not enough
- Our approach: Policy-learn
- Expressiveness advantages, experimental results, contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:

  - promising direction to overcome expressive-power limits of MPNNs (cite)

  - e.g. delete exactly one node, or more generally mark exactly one node, connectivity unchanged (cite)
  - equivariant architecture on the bag, aggregate -> graph- or node-level predictions

- Computational cost

  - intractable on large graphs, can't use on common datasets
  - previous works: randomly sample small subset each epoch (cite); less runtime and cost, still good performance
- Do we need all subgraphs?
  - Figure 1: two non-isomorphic graphs, MPNNs can't distinguish
  - prior work: bags of node-marked subgraphs make them distinguishable (cite)
  - but one subgraph per graph is enough -> constant-sized bags instead of n-sized
- Random selection is not enough
  - in Figure 1 all node-marked subgraphs isomorphic -> random pick works
  - Section 4: families of non-isomorphic graphs where a few carefully chosen subgraphs are sufficient and necessary for WL-indistinguishable graphs
  - probability random baseline picks them -> zero; motivates learning to select
- Policy-learn
  - learn selection policies, far fewer subgraphs, task- and graph-adaptive
  - two Subgraph GNNs: (i) selection network, (ii) downstream prediction network
  - selection network iteratively builds bag; prediction network solves task
  - trained end-to-end on downstream loss; straight-through Gumbel-Softmax estimator (cite) for differentiable sampling
- Advantages and contributions
  - Subgraph GNN as selector + sequential generation -> more expressive than random and previous approaches (cite), more diverse policies
  - proof: can select required subgraphs in those families; previous approaches no better than random
  - experiments: competitive with full-bag, far fewer subgraphs; beats random baselines and previous methods on many tasks
  - contributions: (1) framework; (2) theoretical analysis; (3) experiments, predictive performance + reduced runtime

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Subgraph GNNs are a promising research direction that has recently emerged to get past the expressive-power limitations of Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs). Basically, a Subgraph GNN first turns an input graph into a bag of subgraphs, which are obtained with a predefined generation policy. For example each subgraph could be generated by deleting exactly one node in the original graph, or, more generally, by marking exactly one node in the original graph and leaving the connectivity as it is. Then it applies an equivariant architecture to process the bag of subgraphs, and it aggregates the representations to get graph- or node-level predictions. Subgraph GNNs are popular not only because they have more expressive power than MPNNs but also because they perform remarkably well empirically, for example their success on the ZINC molecular dataset.

The problem is that Subgraph GNNs are computationally expensive, since they do message-passing operations on all the subgraphs in the bag. In the existing subgraph generation policies there are at least as many subgraphs in the bag as there are nodes in the graph (n), and this gives a computational complexity of \mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot d) compared to only \mathcal{O}(n\cdot d) for a standard MPNN, where d is the maximal node degree. This overhead becomes intractable in large graphs, and so Subgraph GNNs can't be applied on commonly-used datasets. To deal with this, previous works have randomly sampled a small subset of subgraphs from the bag in every training epoch, and showed that this significantly reduces the running time and computational cost and still keeps good performance empirically.

So the question is: do we really need to consider all the subgraphs in the bag? To answer this, look at the two non-isomorphic graphs in Figure 1, which MPNNs can't distinguish. Prior work showed that if we encode these graphs as bags of subgraphs, each one obtained by marking a single node, they become distinguishable. But as we can see in the Figure, we don't need all the subgraphs, and we can distinguish the graphs with only one subgraph per graph. So in terms of expressive power, Subgraph GNNs can tell these graphs apart with constant-sized bags, instead of the n -sized bags that existing methods usually use.

- Random selection is not enough
  - in Figure 1 all node-marked subgraphs isomorphic -> random pick works
  - Section 4: families of non-isomorphic graphs where a few carefully chosen subgraphs are sufficient and necessary for WL-indistinguishable graphs
  - probability random baseline picks them -> zero; motivates learning to select
- Policy-learn
  - learn selection policies, far fewer subgraphs, task- and graph-adaptive
  - two Subgraph GNNs: (i) selection network, (ii) downstream prediction network
  - selection network iteratively builds bag; prediction network solves task
  - trained end-to-end on downstream loss; straight-through Gumbel-Softmax estimator (cite) for differentiable sampling
- Advantages and contributions
  - Subgraph GNN as selector + sequential generation -> more expressive than random and previous approaches (cite), more diverse policies
  - proof: can select required subgraphs in those families; previous approaches no better than random
  - experiments: competitive with full-bag, far fewer subgraphs; beats random baselines and previous methods on many tasks
  - contributions: (1) framework; (2) theoretical analysis; (3) experiments, predictive performance + reduced runtime

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Subgraph GNNs are a promising research direction that has recently emerged to get past the expressive-power limitations of Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs). Basically, a Subgraph GNN first turns an input graph into a bag of subgraphs, which are obtained with a predefined generation policy. For example each subgraph could be generated by deleting exactly one node in the original graph, or, more generally, by marking exactly one node in the original graph and leaving the connectivity as it is. Then it applies an equivariant architecture to process the bag of subgraphs, and it aggregates the representations to get graph- or node-level predictions. Subgraph GNNs are popular not only because they have more expressive power than MPNNs but also because they perform remarkably well empirically, for example their success on the ZINC molecular dataset.

The problem is that Subgraph GNNs are computationally expensive, since they do message-passing operations on all the subgraphs in the bag. In the existing subgraph generation policies there are at least as many subgraphs in the bag as there are nodes in the graph (n), and this gives a computational complexity of \mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot d) compared to only \mathcal{O}(n\cdot d) for a standard MPNN, where d is the maximal node degree. This overhead becomes intractable in large graphs, and so Subgraph GNNs can't be applied on commonly-used datasets. To deal with this, previous works have randomly sampled a small subset of subgraphs from the bag in every training epoch, and showed that this significantly reduces the running time and computational cost and still keeps good performance empirically.

So the question is: do we really need to consider all the subgraphs in the bag? To answer this, look at the two non-isomorphic graphs in Figure 1, which MPNNs can't distinguish. Prior work showed that if we encode these graphs as bags of subgraphs, each one obtained by marking a single node, they become distinguishable. But as we can see in the Figure, we don't need all the subgraphs, and we can distinguish the graphs with only one subgraph per graph. So in terms of expressive power, Subgraph GNNs can tell these graphs apart with constant-sized bags, instead of the n -sized bags that existing methods usually use.

The example in Figure 1 shows the potential of subgraph selection policies that return a small number of subgraphs. However, in these two graphs all the node-marked subgraphs are isomorphic, so picking one subgraph at random in each graph is enough to disambiguate them. In Section 4 we generalize this example and prove that there are families of non-isomorphic graphs where a small number of carefully chosen subgraphs is sufficient and necessary for identifying graphs that are otherwise WL-indistinguishable. In these families the probability that a random selection baseline returns the needed subgraphs goes to zero, which motivates learning to select subgraphs instead of choosing them randomly.

In this paper we want to learn subgraph selection policies that return a much smaller number of subgraphs than the total in the bag, and do so in a task- and graph-adaptive way. For this we propose an architecture called Policy-learn, which is made of two Subgraph GNNs: (i) a selection network, and (ii) a downstream prediction network. The selection network learns a subgraph selection policy and builds a bag of subgraphs iteratively. Then this bag is passed to the prediction network, which solves the downstream task we are interested in. The whole architecture is trained end-to-end with the loss function of the downstream task, using the straight-through Gumbel-Softmax estimator so that sampling from the selection policy is differentiable.

We will see that using a Subgraph GNN as the selection network, and the sequential way we generate the policy, give extra expressive power compared to random selection and previous approaches, and let us learn a more diverse set of policies. In particular, we prove that our framework can learn to select the subgraphs needed for disambiguation in the families of graphs mentioned above, while previous approaches provably can't do better than randomly selecting a subset of subgraphs.

In the experiments we show that Policy-learn is competitive with full-bag Subgraph GNNs, even when it learns to select a dramatically smaller number of subgraphs. We also show that it has advantages over random selection baselines and previous methods on a wide range of tasks.

Contributions. The contributions of this paper are: (1) A new framework for learning subgraph selection policies; (2) A theoretical analysis that motivates the policy learning task and our architecture; and (3) An experimental evaluation of the new approach that shows its advantages in predictive performance and reduced runtime.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Subgraph GNNs [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9] have recently emerged as a promising research direction for overcoming the expressive-power limitations of Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) [10,11]. In essence, a Subgraph GNN first transforms an input graph into a bag of subgraphs, obtained according to a predefined generation policy. For instance, each subgraph might be generated by deleting exactly one node in the original graph, or, more generally, by marking exactly one node in the original graph while leaving the connectivity unaltered [6]. It then applies an equivariant architecture to process the bag of subgraphs, and aggregates the representations to obtain graph- or node-level predictions. The popularity of Subgraph GNNs is due not only to their increased expressive power compared to MPNNs but also to their remarkable empirical performance, as exemplified by their success on the ZINC molecular dataset [7,9].

Unfortunately, Subgraph GNNs are hampered by their computational cost, since they perform message-passing operations on all subgraphs within the bag. In existing subgraph generation policies, the bag contains at least as many subgraphs as there are nodes in the graph (n), which leads to a computational complexity of \mathcal{O}(n^{2}\cdot d), compared to just \mathcal{O}(n\cdot d) for a standard MPNN, where d represents the maximal node degree. This overhead becomes intractable in large graphs, preventing Subgraph GNNs from being applied to commonly-used datasets. To address this limitation, previous works [2,4,5] have randomly sampled a small subset of subgraphs from the bag in every training epoch, showing that this approach significantly reduces the running time and computational cost while empirically retaining good performance.

This raises the following question: is it really necessary to consider all the subgraphs in the bag? To answer it, consider the two non-isomorphic graphs in Figure 1, which MPNNs cannot distinguish. As shown by prior work [2], encoding such graphs as bags of subgraphs, each obtained by marking a single node, makes them distinguishable. However, as the Figure shows, using all subgraphs is unnecessary: distinguishability can be achieved with only one subgraph per graph. Thus, from the standpoint of expressive power, Subgraph GNNs can distinguish these graphs using constant-sized bags, rather than the n -sized bags typically used by existing methods.

The example in Figure 1 shows the potential of subgraph selection policies that return a small number of subgraphs. However, since all node-marked subgraphs in these two graphs are isomorphic, randomly selecting one subgraph in each graph is enough for disambiguation. In Section 4 we generalize this example and prove that there exist families of non-isomorphic graphs where a small number of carefully chosen subgraphs is sufficient and necessary for identifying otherwise WL-indistinguishable graphs. In these families, the probability that a random selection baseline returns the required subgraphs tends to zero, which motivates learning to select subgraphs rather than choosing them randomly.

In this paper, we aim to learn subgraph selection policies that return a significantly smaller number of subgraphs than the total available in the bag, in a task- and graph-adaptive fashion. To that end, we propose an architecture, called Policy-learn, composed of two Subgraph GNNs: (i) a selection network, and (ii) a downstream prediction network. The selection network learns a subgraph selection policy and iteratively constructs a bag of subgraphs, which is then passed to the prediction network to solve the downstream task of interest. The complete architecture is trained end-to-end according to the downstream task’s loss function, using the straight-through Gumbel-Softmax estimator [12,13] to allow differentiable sampling from the selection policy.

As we shall see, our choice of a Subgraph GNN as the selection network, together with the sequential nature of our policy generation, provides additional expressive power compared to random selection and previous approaches [8], and allows us to learn a more diverse set of policies. Specifically, we prove that our framework can learn to select the subgraphs required for disambiguation in the families of graphs mentioned above, whereas previous approaches provably cannot do better than randomly selecting a subset of subgraphs.

Experimentally, we show that Policy-learn is competitive with full-bag Subgraph GNNs, even when it learns to select a dramatically smaller number of subgraphs. We further demonstrate its advantages over random selection baselines and previous methods on a wide range of tasks.

Contributions. This paper makes the following contributions: (1) A new framework for learning subgraph selection policies; (2) A theoretical analysis motivating the policy learning task as well as our architecture; and (3) An experimental evaluation of the new approach showing its advantages in terms of predictive performance and reduced runtime.
